clue.text: Mia Klein periodically visited country

indicators.note: at regular intervals: take every other letter

explanation.surface: A woman named Mia Klein goes abroad now and then.
explanation.walkthrough: Mia Klein is nobody; the name exists only to supply letters. Count the space as nothing: M, A, L, I are the 1st, 3rd, 5th and 7th letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Mali is one of many countries, a landlocked state in West Africa.

clue.text: Smuggle in a cutting implement

indicators.note: one piece is placed inside another

parts.note: a = per, as in 'ten pounds a head'
to run guns or drugs is to smuggle them

explanation.surface: Someone sneaks a blade past customs.
explanation.walkthrough: The little word 'a' does real work here: 'a' and 'per' are interchangeable in prices, so it supplies PER to hold RUN.
explanation.definitionFit: A pruner is a tool for cutting back plants.

clue.text: Good law easing supply for Govan native

indicators.note: read as the adverb of 'supple': bendily, so the letters are bent into a new order

parts.note: G = good, the standard abbreviation, rearranged along with the rest

explanation.surface: A kinder law is brought in to help a man from Glasgow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Supply' looks like a noun, as in provision, but it is the adverb 'supply' (in a supple way). Govan is a district of Glasgow on the Clyde.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone born in Govan is born in Glasgow, so is a Glaswegian.

clue.text: Drink in sailor's world?

parts.note: AB = able seaman, a sailor, plus the 's
the orb = the globe, the world

explanation.surface: A question about what a sailor gets to drink in his world.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drink in' reads as drinking inside somewhere, but it is one phrasal verb, meaning to take in eagerly.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: taking in a view or a lecture eagerly is soaking it up.

clue.text: Cook hake endlessly and broil some greens

indicators.note: to cook something up is to alter or rework it, so the letters are mixed
endlessly means the last letter of hake is dropped

explanation.surface: A recipe: prepare the fish, grill it, and serve some vegetables.
explanation.walkthrough: HAK (hake without its end) and BROIL are mixed by 'Cook'.
explanation.definitionFit: Kohlrabi is a cabbage-family vegetable with an edible swollen stem and leafy tops.

clue.text: Saint Christopher's parody

parts.note: Kit is a pet form of Christopher; the 's is 'has', joining to the definition

explanation.surface: A reference to a mocking piece about St Christopher.
explanation.walkthrough: Saint Christopher looks like one name, the patron of travellers, but it splits into S and a nickname for Christopher.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a short comic sketch mocking something is a parody.

clue.text: Hot tub with two males excited little fellow

indicators.note: stirred up, so the letters are agitated into a new order

explanation.surface: A hot tub with two men in it sets a small chap aflutter.
explanation.walkthrough: Tom Thumb is the thumb-sized hero of an English folk tale.
explanation.definitionFit: Tom Thumb, no bigger than a thumb, is the archetypal little fellow.

clue.text: Send fresh fish minus tail for broadcaster

indicators.note: fresh suggests the word Send made anew, so its letters are rearranged
minus tail tells us to drop the final letter of the fish

explanation.surface: An instruction to post out fresh fish, with the tail cut off, to someone on the radio.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fresh' rearranges SEND into NEDS; 'minus tail' docks HERRING to HERRIN. Ned Sherrin was a British broadcaster, satirist and producer, long the host of Radio 4's Loose Ends.
explanation.definitionFit: Ned Sherrin presented radio and television programmes for decades, so he is an example of a broadcaster.

clue.text: Eliot's cruellest month lands pair in trouble

indicators.note: lands ... in means puts one thing into another, so the pair goes inside the trouble
in completes 'lands ... in', placing the pair inside the trouble word

parts.note: to ail is to trouble or afflict

explanation.surface: T. S. Eliot's grim month brings problems for a couple.
explanation.walkthrough: The Waste Land opens 'April is the cruellest month'. Here 'trouble' is the verb AIL, not a noun.
explanation.definitionFit: The first line of Eliot's poem calls the fourth month of the year the cruellest, a famous literary quotation.

clue.text: City area veto damaged union privilege

parts.note: a block is an area of a city bounded by streets

indicators.note: damaged suggests the word veto broken up, so its letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A city district where a ban has been spoiled by trade unionists' special rights.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Damaged' turns VETO into VOTE. A block vote lets a delegate, typically a trade union leader, cast the votes of all the members represented at once.
explanation.definitionFit: Casting many members' votes as one bloc is a power historically held by trade unions at Labour Party conferences.

clue.text: Dramatist jokes amongst current company

indicators.note: placed in the middle of other letters

parts.note: 'that's a good one' — a one is a joke

explanation.surface: A playwright's humour goes down well with a theatre company of the day.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Current company' reads as a present-day troupe; it is two abbreviations, I and CO, with ONES tucked between. Eugène Ionesco wrote absurdist plays such as Rhinoceros.
explanation.definitionFit: Eugène Ionesco was a Romanian-French dramatist.

clue.text: Understatement from one devoured by 50 bears?

indicators.note: swallowed up inside what follows

parts.note: to tote = to carry, to bear

explanation.surface: Saying fifty bears ate someone would be an understatement, the question mark admits.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bears' is not the animals but a verb, carries; I goes inside L+TOTES. Litotes is understatement by negation: 'not bad' for good.
explanation.definitionFit: Litotes is the figure of speech that makes a point by understating it.

clue.text: European republic in revolution inspiring unease

indicators.note: turned round, so read backwards

explanation.surface: A European state in the grip of a revolt causes anxiety.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In revolution' suggests political upheaval; it only means turn round. Eire is the Irish name for the Republic of Ireland.
explanation.definitionFit: Something eerie is strange in a way that makes one uneasy.

clue.text: Where daddy treated murderous alter ego

indicators.note: processed, so the letters are worked into a new order

explanation.surface: A question about where a father took a killer's other self for a meal.
explanation.walkthrough: Mr Edward Hyde is the murderous other self of Dr Jekyll in Stevenson's novella.
explanation.definitionFit: Hyde is the alter ego Dr Jekyll turns into, and he commits murder.

clue.text: Duck in city by river and building thereon

indicators.note: by means next to, so the river name is placed right after the city piece
in means the duck letter is placed inside the city name

parts.note: a duck is a score of nothing in cricket, so O
the Ouse is an English river

explanation.surface: A duck swimming in a city near a river, with a building on the water.
explanation.walkthrough: O goes in BATH, then OUSE follows. Bath is a city in south-west England; the Ouse is a river.
explanation.definitionFit: A boathouse is a shed built at the water's edge or over a river to store boats.

clue.text: Fanatical sort in old car following van

indicators.note: comes after, so this piece goes second

parts.note: the van (vanguard) is the head, the front
a banger is a battered old car

explanation.surface: A zealot is riding in an old car behind a van.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Van' is the vehicle in the surface, but it means the front, as in vanguard. A banger is British slang for a clapped-out car.
explanation.definitionFit: A headbanger is a wild-eyed zealot, a fanatic.

clue.text: Nimble Warwick is strangely optimistic character

indicators.note: oddly arranged, so the letters are reordered

explanation.surface: A person called Warwick, quick on his feet, is an odd kind of cheerful figure.
explanation.walkthrough: Wilkins Micawber in Dickens's David Copperfield is forever sure that 'something will turn up'.
explanation.definitionFit: Mr Micawber is literature's byword for hopeless optimism.

clue.text: Syrian neighbour curses in shelter

indicators.note: one piece goes inside another

parts.note: the lee is the sheltered side

explanation.surface: Someone next door to Syria swears as they take cover.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Curses' reads as swearing; it is a noun, banes.
explanation.definitionFit: Lebanon borders Syria, so a Lebanese person is a Syrian's neighbour.

clue.text: Stakes raised for the defence?

definitions.meaning: not bets increased, but wooden posts stood upright in a row
not a lawyer's case, but protection against attack; the question mark flags the double reading

explanation.surface: A gambler, or a lawyer, ups the stakes to help the defence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stakes raised' sounds like a bigger bet and 'the defence' like a court case; literally they are posts stood upright to keep attackers out.
explanation.definitionFit: A stockade is a barrier of upright stakes put up for defence.

clue.text: Outlaw cross about wine store next to house

indicators.note: around, so the cross wraps what follows

parts.note: a rood is a cross, as in rood screen

indicators.note: beside, so the two pieces are joined

parts.note: a wine bin, a rack for storing bottles

explanation.surface: A bandit, angered by a cellar beside a home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cross' looks like angry, but it is the noun: a rood is the cross in a church. A wine bin is a rack for bottles.
explanation.definitionFit: Robin Hood is the legendary outlaw of Sherwood Forest.

clue.text: Period outside court on left foot

indicators.note: on in a down clue means the first piece sits on top of the left letter
outside means the word for period goes around the court abbreviation

parts.note: a day is a period of time

explanation.surface: A spell outside the courtroom standing on one's left foot.
explanation.walkthrough: DAY goes outside CT; in a down clue L sits on (below) it.
explanation.definitionFit: A dactyl is a metrical foot of one stressed syllable followed by two unstressed ones.

clue.text: Romantic writer in past first to leave club

parts.note: by can mean past, as in 'walk by'

indicators.note: first to leave means the opening letter of the club goes

parts.note: an iron is a golf club

explanation.surface: A Romantic author who once had to resign first from a club.
explanation.walkthrough: 'First to leave' takes the I from IRON. Lord Byron was one of the great English Romantic poets.
explanation.definitionFit: Byron belongs to the Romantic movement of English poetry, alongside Shelley and Keats.

clue.text: Attacker, one helping to support Resistance

indicators.note: in a down clue, a supporter sits underneath

explanation.surface: An assailant, an ally who backs the wartime Resistance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Resistance' has the wartime movement in mind; it is simply R. In a down entry what supports comes below.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: one who makes a raid is an attacker.

clue.text: Bully ambassador parking in constricted space

parts.note: HE = His Excellency, an ambassador's title

indicators.note: one piece goes inside another

parts.note: a neck is a narrow passage, as of a bottle

explanation.surface: An envoy is harassed about parking in a tight spot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bully' looks like a noun but the answer is a verb: to henpeck is to nag and domineer.
explanation.definitionFit: To henpeck someone, usually a husband, is to bully them with constant nagging.

clue.text: Value reflected welcoming a wronged brother

indicators.note: mirrored, so read backwards
taking in, so it wraps what follows

parts.note: use = value, as in 'of little use'

explanation.surface: Thinking over what a mistreated sibling was worth.
explanation.walkthrough: Esau, in Genesis, was cheated of his birthright and blessing by his twin brother Jacob.
explanation.definitionFit: Esau was wronged by his brother Jacob, who took his blessing.

clue.text: Satire performed — stick around

indicators.note: wraps round the piece before it

explanation.surface: A satirical piece is staged with a walking stick as a prop.
explanation.walkthrough: The dash suggests a stage direction; 'around' at the end tells the stick to wrap what comes before it. Candide is Voltaire's 1759 satire.
explanation.definitionFit: Candide is Voltaire's satire on philosophical optimism.

clue.text: Scratching head, Kerouac and Ginsberg scoff

indicators.note: the head, first letter, is struck out

parts.note: Jack Kerouac and Allen Ginsberg were Beat writers, BEATS; drop the B

explanation.surface: Two puzzled Beat poets sneer at something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scoff' looks like mockery, which suits the poets; it is the British slang sense, to eat greedily.
explanation.definitionFit: To scoff is to eat hungrily, so he scoffs = he eats.

clue.text: Despicable celeb in pop lady cleaned out

indicators.note: one piece goes inside another
emptied of the middle, leaving the outer letters

explanation.surface: A contemptible celebrity featured in a pop song about a woman down on her luck.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pop' tempts as music, beside 'celeb'; it is a father, DAD.
explanation.definitionFit: Dastardly means wicked and contemptible.

clue.text: Put out in Paris, I recalled shocking treatment

indicators.note: called back, so read backwards

explanation.surface: Someone upset in Paris remembers harsh treatment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shocking' sounds like outrage; it is literal, the electric-shock therapy ECT.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to put out a troublemaker is to throw them out.
